pages.summary: Geometric transformations of the plane: affine and projective, by row-vector or column-vector matrices.
body: An affine transformation maps lines to lines and keeps parallels parallel (rotation, scaling, shear, translation); a projective one maps lines to lines but not parallels to parallels (a perspective view). `affine2d` and `projective2d` hold T for row vectors, [u v 1] = [x y 1] T; `affinetform2d` and `projtform2d` hold A = T' for column vectors, [u; v; 1] = A [x; y; 1]. `transformPointsForward` and `transformPointsInverse` take points through them, `invert` gives the inverse, `outputLimits` where a rectangle goes, and `imwarp` transforms images.

examples.title: A shear and a perspective

pages.summary: Transformations of fewer kinds: rigid motions, similarities and translations, and tests for the kind.
body: `rigidtform2d` is a rotation (theta degrees, counterclockwise as the axes go: x right, y down) and a translation; `simtform2d` adds a scale; `transltform2d` is a translation alone. Their properties give the angle, scale and translation directly. `isTranslation`, `isRigid` and `isSimilarity` test any transformation.

examples.title: Kinds told apart

pages.summary: Points taken through a transformation and back, its inverse, and where a rectangle goes.
body: `transformPointsForward` gives the points u, v a transformation takes x, y to (as two arrays, or as rows of a matrix); `transformPointsInverse` takes them back. `invert` gives the inverse transformation. `outputLimits` gives the bounding box of a rectangle's image (its edges sampled for a projective transformation), which is where `imwarp` puts its output.

examples.title: There and back

pages.summary: Where an image lies in world coordinates.
body: By default pixel (r, c) is at x = c, y = r: the image spans [0.5, n + 0.5] by [0.5, m + 0.5]. Given world limits or a pixel size, each pixel has a place in world units (metres, say). `worldToIntrinsic` and `intrinsicToWorld` convert between the two, `worldToSubscript` gives the row and column holding a point (NaN outside), and `sizesMatch` tests an image's size. `imwarp` and `imshow` take a reference.

examples.title: An image of 0.5 m pixels
examples.code:
R = imref2d([40 60], 0.5, 0.5)
[xw, yw] = intrinsicToWorld(R, 60, 40)
[r, c] = worldToSubscript(R, [10 100], [5 5])
[xi, yi] = worldToIntrinsic(R, 10, 5)
sizesMatch(R, zeros(40, 60))

body: Each output pixel takes the value at the inverse image of its centre (`'linear'` interpolation by default, `'nearest'` or `'cubic'`), `'FillValues'` (0) outside. The output covers the whole transformed image at the input's pixel size, with its own reference (the second output), unless `'OutputView'` gives one, for instance the input's, to keep the frame. A displacement field D (m-by-n-by-2) instead moves each pixel by its own amount.
syntax: B = imwarp(A, tform, interp, 'OutputView', Rout, 'FillValues', v)

examples.title: A phantom turned, sheared, and warped by a field

pages.summary: A transformation fitted to pairs of matching points.
body: By least squares from the moving points onto the fixed ones: `fitgeotform2d` fits `'rigid'`, `'similarity'`, `'affine'` or `'projective'` transformations (the column-vector kinds); `fitgeotrans` fits `'nonreflectivesimilarity'`, `'similarity'` (a reflection allowed), `'affine'` or `'projective'` (the row-vector kinds). A projective fit needs at least four pairs, an affine one three, a similarity two.

examples.title: A known motion recovered from noisy points

pages.summary: Images registered by phase correlation: the transformation that takes one onto another.
body: The normalized cross power spectrum of the two images peaks at their relative shift (`'translation'`, to a fraction of a pixel); for `'rigid'` and `'similarity'` (the default) the rotation and scale come first from the log-polar magnitude spectra (Fourier-Mellin). The images are tapered first unless `'Window'` is false. The result takes the moving image onto the fixed one, as `imwarp` uses it.
syntax: Of a kind, with the peak's height.

examples.title: A shifted and turned copy found
examples.intro: The transformation found takes the copy back onto the original: its inverse is the motion that made the copy.
